prescriptions.name: Acne Vulgaris
prescriptions.summary: Acne vulgaris is a common chronic inflammatory skin condition involving the pilosebaceous units. It commonly presents with comedones, papules, pustules, nodules, and scarring, often on the face, chest, and back. Treatment is tailored to severity and may include topical agents, oral antibiotics, and adjunctive skincare.

regimens.name: Oral Antibiotic + Topical Therapy
regimens.description: Combination therapy for moderate-severe inflammatory acne. Oral doxycycline provides systemic anti-inflammatory and antibacterial effects. Azelaic acid and benzoyl peroxide provide topical action.

medications.name: Doxycycline 100 mg
medications.sig: 1 capsule once daily with food for 12 weeks

medications.name: Azelaic Acid 15% cream
medications.sig: Apply thin layer to affected areas twice daily for 12 weeks

medications.name: Benzoyl Peroxide 2.5% gel
medications.sig: Apply thin layer to affected areas at bedtime for 12 weeks

highlights.label: Photosensitivity
highlights.text: Doxycycline causes photosensitivity. Strict sun protection with SPF 50+ sunscreen essential. Avoid prolonged sun exposure and tanning beds.

highlights.label: GI Side Effects
highlights.text: Take doxycycline with food to minimize GI distress. Remain upright for 30 minutes after taking to prevent esophagitis. Monitor for nausea, diarrhea.

highlights.label: Expected Timeline
highlights.text: Expect gradual improvement over 6-8 weeks. Adherence to full 12-week course is important. Continue topical maintenance after stopping oral antibiotic.

regimens.name: Topical Only Maintenance
regimens.description: For mild acne or after completing oral antibiotic course. Focuses on topical maintenance to prevent recurrence.

medications.name: Azelaic Acid 15% cream
medications.sig: Apply thin layer to affected areas twice daily

medications.name: Acne Soap (salicylic acid based)
medications.sig: Wash face twice daily

medications.name: Sunscreen SPF 30+
medications.sig: Apply daily before sun exposure

highlights.label: Maintenance
highlights.text: Continue topical therapy even after acne clears to prevent recurrence. Sunscreen is essential for post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation prevention.

prescriptions.name: Melasma
prescriptions.summary: Melasma is an acquired hyperpigmentation disorder characterized by symmetric, blotchy brownish macules on sun-exposed areas, particularly the face. It is more common in females and darker skin types. Management involves photoprotection, topical depigmenting agents, and procedural therapies. Treatment is stepwise and requires long-term maintenance due to high recurrence rates.

regimens.name: Triple Combination Therapy
regimens.description: First-line therapy for melasma. Triple combination cream with hydroquinone, tretinoin, and fluocinolone is the gold standard. Limited to 8 weeks due to hydroquinone risks.

medications.name: Hydroquinone 4% + Tretinoin 0.05% + Fluocinolone 0.01% cream
medications.sig: Apply thin layer to affected facial areas ONCE daily at bedtime (max 8 weeks)

medications.name: Sunscreen SPF 50+ (tinted preferred)
medications.sig: Apply daily, reapply every 2-3 hours

highlights.label: Duration Limit
highlights.text: Hydroquinone is limited to 8 weeks of continuous use. Longer use may cause ochronosis (blue-black pigmentation). After 8 weeks, switch to maintenance therapy.

highlights.label: Sun Protection
highlights.text: Strict photoprotection is CRITICAL. Tinted sunscreen provides visible light protection which is important for melasma. Reapply every 2-3 hours.

highlights.label: Skin Irritation
highlights.text: Tretinoin causes irritation, peeling, and redness initially. Start with alternate nights if sensitive. Use moisturizer during the day.

highlights.label: Expected Response
highlights.text: Improvement visible at 4-8 weeks. Complete response may require 12-16 weeks. Maintenance required lifelong.

regimens.name: Maintenance Therapy
regimens.description: After stopping hydroquinone, maintain results with azelaic acid, kojic acid, or other depigmenting agents. Sun protection remains essential.

medications.name: Azelaic acid 15-20% cream
medications.sig: Apply twice daily (maintenance after stopping hydroquinone)

medications.name: Kojic acid 2% / Tranexamic acid 3% serum
medications.sig: Apply twice daily (alternative maintenance)

highlights.label: Recurrence Risk
highlights.text: Melasma has high recurrence rates. Consistent maintenance therapy and sun protection are essential. Pulse hydroquinone courses may be needed.

highlights.label: Long-term Strategy
highlights.text: Maintenance cream + daily sunscreen + pulse hydroquinone courses as needed. Assess epidermal vs dermal vs mixed pattern using Wood's lamp.

regimens.name: Refractory Melasma
regimens.description: For refractory cases not responding to topical therapy. Adds oral tranexamic acid which inhibits plasminogen activation and reduces melanogenesis.

medications.name: Tranexamic acid 250 mg
medications.sig: 1 tablet twice daily for 8-12 weeks (refractory cases)

medications.name: Azelaic acid 15-20% cream
medications.sig: Continue maintenance cream

highlights.label: Thrombosis Risk
highlights.text: Tranexamic acid increases thrombotic risk. Contraindicated in patients with history of DVT, PE, or hypercoagulable states. Use with caution.

highlights.label: GI Side Effects
highlights.text: Oral tranexamic acid may cause nausea, GI upset. Take with food. Rarely causes visual disturbances.

highlights.label: Alternative Options
highlights.text: If inadequate at 12 weeks: Consider PRP injections, gentle chemical peels, or low-fluence laser (dermatologist only).

prescriptions.name: Acute Cystitis (Pregnant Patient)
prescriptions.summary: Acute cystitis in pregnancy is a common bacterial infection of the bladder that requires prompt antibiotic treatment to prevent complications such as pyelonephritis and preterm labor. Asymptomatic bacteriuria also requires treatment in pregnancy. Antibiotic selection must consider fetal safety, with fosfomycin and nitrofurantoin as first-line options, avoiding nitrofurantoin near term. Urine culture is essential to guide therapy, and test-of-cure is recommended.

regimens.name: First-Line Fosfomycin
regimens.description: Single-dose fosfomycin has the highest cure rate for acute cystitis. Safe in pregnancy with excellent efficacy. Preferred for simple cystitis.

medications.name: Fosfomycin trometamol 3g sachet
medications.sig: Dissolve in 50-100 ml water. Take as a single dose NOW.

highlights.label: Urine Culture
highlights.text: Send urine culture (midstream) BEFORE antibiotic. Test-of-cure urine culture 1-2 weeks after treatment completion.

highlights.label: Hydration
highlights.text: Encourage increased fluid intake. Hydration and urinary alkalinization may provide symptomatic relief.

highlights.label: Expected Response
highlights.text: Symptom improvement within 24-48 hours. If no improvement, consider alternative diagnosis or resistant organism.

highlights.label: Refer Criteria
highlights.text: REFER IF: Fever >38°C, flank pain, no improvement after 48 hours, vomiting. Consider admission for parenteral antibiotics if pyelonephritis suspected.

regimens.name: Nitrofurantoin 7-Day Course
regimens.description: Alternative first-line if fosfomycin unavailable. Safe in pregnancy but contraindicated near term (38-42 weeks) due to risk of neonatal hemolysis.

medications.name: Nitrofurantoin 100 mg
medications.sig: 1 capsule twice daily for 7 days (if fosfomycin unavailable; avoid at term 38-42 weeks)

highlights.label: Gestational Age Check
highlights.text: Avoid nitrofurantoin at term (38-42 weeks) due to risk of neonatal hemolysis. Confirm gestational age before prescribing.

highlights.label: GI Side Effects
highlights.text: Take with food to reduce nausea. Monitor for GI upset.

highlights.label: Alternative
highlights.text: If nitrofurantoin contraindicated, use cephalexin 500mg QID × 7 days.

regimens.name: Cephalexin 7-Day Course
regimens.description: Second-line option if nitrofurantoin contraindicated (at term) or fosfomycin unavailable. Safe in pregnancy.

medications.name: Cephalexin 500 mg
medications.sig: 1 capsule four times daily for 7 days (second-line if nitrofurantoin contraindicated)

highlights.label: Safe Alternative
highlights.text: Cephalexin is a safe second-line option in pregnancy. Category B. Effective for E. coli and other common uropathogens.

highlights.label: Compliance
highlights.text: Four times daily dosing may affect compliance. Consider prescribing longer course for reliable patients.

prescriptions.name: Acute Tonsillitis (Pregnant - Penicillin Allergy)
prescriptions.summary: Acute tonsillitis in pregnancy is an inflammatory infection of the palatine tonsils, commonly caused by group A Streptococcus (GAS). For penicillin-allergic pregnant patients without anaphylactic reaction, cephalexin is the first-line alternative. Erythromycin is the preferred macrolide in pregnancy due to extensive safety data. Azithromycin may be used if other options are unavailable. Supportive care with paracetamol, saline gargles, and hydration is essential. Monitor for complications and refer for suppurative complications or airway compromise.

regimens.name: Cephalexin 7-10 Day Course
regimens.description: First-line for penicillin-allergic pregnant patients without anaphylactic reaction. Cephalexin is safe and effective for GAS tonsillitis.

medications.name: Cephalexin 500 mg
medications.sig: 1 capsule FOUR times daily (every 6 hours) for 7-10 days (Pregnancy Category B)

medications.name: Paracetamol 500 mg
medications.sig: As needed for pain/fever (safe in pregnancy)

highlights.label: Penicillin Allergy Type
highlights.text: Cephalexin is safe for non-anaphylactic penicillin allergy. If anaphylactic reaction history, avoid cephalosporins and use erythromycin instead.

highlights.label: Refer Criteria
highlights.text: REFER IF: Difficulty breathing or stridor, inability to swallow saliva (drooling), muffled voice (hot potato voice), unilateral tonsillar swelling pushing uvula, fever >39°C for >48 hours, dehydration.

highlights.label: Throat Swab
highlights.text: Consider throat swab for culture if no improvement at 5-7 days.

highlights.label: Expected Outcome
highlights.text: 24-48 hours: Significant symptom improvement; 7-10 days: Complete resolution.

regimens.followUp: 5-7 days (if no improvement, consider throat swab and culture)

regimens.name: Erythromycin 7-10 Day Course
regimens.description: Preferred macrolide in pregnancy with most documented experience. Use if cephalexin contraindicated or patient has anaphylactic penicillin allergy.

medications.name: Erythromycin 500 mg
medications.sig: 1 tablet FOUR times daily for 7-10 days (Pregnancy Category B)

medications.name: Paracetamol 500 mg
medications.sig: As needed for pain/fever

highlights.label: GI Side Effects
highlights.text: Erythromycin commonly causes GI upset. Take with food. Consider dividing doses or using enteric-coated formulation.

highlights.label: Drug Interactions
highlights.text: Erythromycin interacts with many drugs (CYP3A4 inhibitor). Check for interactions with other medications.

regimens.name: Azithromycin 3-Day Course
regimens.description: Use only if cephalexin and erythromycin unavailable. Azithromycin is not first-line for Strep pyogenes but can be used if other options unavailable.

medications.name: Azithromycin 500 mg
medications.sig: 1 tablet ONCE daily for 3 days (use only if cephalexin and erythromycin unavailable)

highlights.label: Not First-line
highlights.text: Azithromycin is not first-line for Strep pyogenes. Use only if other options unavailable. Lower cure rate for GAS compared to beta-lactams.

highlights.label: Advantage
highlights.text: Short 3-day course improves compliance. Well-tolerated with once-daily dosing.

prescriptions.name: Scabies
prescriptions.summary: Scabies is a highly contagious parasitic infestation caused by Sarcoptes scabiei var. hominis, characterized by intense nocturnal pruritus and burrows in interdigital spaces, wrists, and flexural areas. Diagnosis is clinical, with burrow identification and family history being key. Treatment involves topical permethrin 5% cream as first-line, with ivermectin for refractory or crusted cases. All household contacts must be treated simultaneously to prevent reinfestation. Environmental decontamination is essential for cure.

regimens.name: Permethrin 5% Cream (Two Applications)
regimens.description: First-line treatment for scabies. Apply to entire body from neck to toes. Two applications 7 days apart kills mites and eggs.

medications.name: Permethrin 5% cream
medications.sig: Apply to entire body from neck to toes (including under nails, between fingers/toes, groin, buttocks, soles). Leave 8-12 hours. Wash off. Repeat after 7 days.

medications.name: Cetirizine 10 mg
medications.sig: 1 tablet daily for 2-4 weeks (for itching)

highlights.label: All Household Contacts
highlights.text: All household contacts must be treated simultaneously regardless of symptoms. Failure to treat contacts causes reinfestation.

highlights.label: Environmental Decontamination
highlights.text: Hot water wash (≥50°C/122°F) for bedding, clothes, towels. Seal non-washable items in plastic bag for 1 week. Vacuum carpets and furniture.

highlights.label: Persistent Pruritus
highlights.text: Pruritus may persist for 2-4 weeks due to hypersensitivity reaction even after successful treatment. This does not mean treatment failed.

highlights.label: Expected Outcome
highlights.text: Mites killed after 1st application. Complete cure after 2 applications (days 1 and 7-14).

highlights.label: Safety
highlights.text: Permethrin is safe in pregnancy and children >2 months.

regimens.followUp: 2 weeks (assess response), 4 weeks (if no improvement, reassess)

regimens.name: Ivermectin (Refractory/Crusted Scabies)
regimens.description: For refractory cases, crusted scabies, immunocompromised patients, or when topical treatment fails. Oral ivermectin is effective and convenient.

medications.name: Ivermectin 200 mcg/kg
medications.sig: Single dose (weight-based). Repeat after 7-14 days if needed (for refractory/crusted scabies).

highlights.label: Pregnancy Category C
highlights.text: Ivermectin is pregnancy category C. Use only when benefits outweigh risks. Avoid in pregnancy if possible.

highlights.label: Crusted Scabies
highlights.text: Crusted scabies requires multiple doses of ivermectin (day 1, 7, and 14). May need combination with topical permethrin. Refer to dermatologist.

highlights.label: Drug Interactions
highlights.text: Avoid concurrent use with other CNS-active drugs. Use with caution in patients with liver disease or on warfarin.

highlights.label: Indication
highlights.text: REFER IF: Crusted scabies, immunocompromised patient, no improvement after 2 cycles, secondary bacterial infection.

prescriptions.name: Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID)
prescriptions.summary: Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID) is an infection of the upper female genital tract, including the uterus, fallopian tubes, and ovaries, typically caused by ascending organisms from the lower tract (Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Chlamydia trachomatis, and anaerobic bacteria). Classic presentation includes bilateral lower abdominal pain, adnexal tenderness, cervical motion tenderness, fever, and abnormal vaginal discharge. Prompt antibiotic treatment is essential to prevent complications such as infertility, ectopic pregnancy, and chronic pelvic pain. Empiric broad-spectrum therapy covering gonorrhea, chlamydia, and anaerobes is recommended.

regimens.name: Cephalosporin-Based Regimen
regimens.description: First-line empiric therapy for PID. Ceftriaxone IM covers gonorrhea, doxycycline covers chlamydia, metronidazole covers anaerobes. Broad-spectrum coverage for all common pathogens.

medications.name: Ceftriaxone 1g IM
medications.sig: Single dose

medications.name: Doxycycline 100 mg
medications.sig: 1 tablet twice daily for 14 days

medications.name: Metronidazole 400 mg
medications.sig: 1 tablet twice daily for 14 days

highlights.label: Partner Treatment
highlights.text: Treat all partners within 60 days. Screen for HIV, syphilis, and other STIs. Avoid sexual intercourse until treatment completed and symptoms resolved.

highlights.label: Hospitalization Criteria
highlights.text: Hospitalize if: pregnant, severe illness, suspected surgical emergency, tubo-ovarian abscess, inability to tolerate oral medications, or lack of response after 72 hours.

highlights.label: Pregnancy Test
highlights.text: Consider pregnancy test in all reproductive-age women before treatment.

highlights.label: IUD Removal
highlights.text: Consider IUD removal if symptoms persist after 72 hours.

highlights.label: Test of Cure
highlights.text: Test of cure not routinely recommended for chlamydia/gonorrhea unless symptoms persist or pregnancy. Repeat testing in 3-6 months due to high reinfection rates.

regimens.name: Fluoroquinolone-Based Regimen
regimens.description: Second-line for patients allergic to cephalosporins or when cephalosporins unavailable. Levofloxacin provides gonorrhea and chlamydia coverage.

medications.name: Levofloxacin 500 mg
medications.sig: 1 tablet once daily for 14 days

medications.name: Metronidazole 500 mg
medications.sig: 1 tablet twice daily for 14 days

highlights.label: Fluoroquinolone Resistance
highlights.text: Increasing gonococcal resistance to fluoroquinolones. Use only if cephalosporin contraindicated or local resistance rates <5%.

highlights.label: Tendon Risk
highlights.text: Fluoroquinolones increase risk of tendonitis and tendon rupture. Avoid in patients >60 years, on corticosteroids, or with renal impairment.

regimens.name: Parenteral (IV) Regimen
regimens.description: For severe PID requiring hospitalization. IV antibiotics followed by oral doxycycline to complete 14-day course.

medications.name: Cefotetan 2g IV
medications.sig: Every 12 hours (switch to oral doxycycline after 24-48 hrs), total 14 days

medications.name: Doxycycline 100 mg
medications.sig: Switch to oral doxycycline 100mg BID to complete 14 days

highlights.label: Hospitalization Required
highlights.text: For severe illness, tubo-ovarian abscess, pregnancy, inability to tolerate oral, or no response to outpatient therapy.

highlights.label: Alternative IV Regimen
highlights.text: Alternative: Clindamycin 900mg IV q8h + Gentamicin 2mg/kg IV/IM loading then 1.5mg/kg IV/IM q8h (switch to oral doxycycline 100mg BID to complete 14 days).

prescriptions.name: Abnormal Uterine Bleeding (AUB-O - Ovulatory Dysfunction)
prescriptions.summary: Abnormal Uterine Bleeding (AUB) is a common gynecological condition characterized by irregular, heavy, or prolonged menstrual bleeding in the absence of structural pathology. In ovulatory dysfunction (AUB-O), bleeding results from anovulation or oligo-ovulation, leading to unopposed estrogen stimulation and endometrial instability. Diagnosis is clinical with normal pelvic exam and negative pregnancy test. Medical management focuses on controlling acute bleeding, regulating menstrual cycles, and preventing recurrence. The combination of tranexamic acid and combined oral contraceptives is highly effective, with tranexamic acid reducing blood loss by 40-60%.

regimens.name: Acute Bleeding Control
regimens.description: First-line for acute heavy menstrual bleeding. Tranexamic acid reduces blood loss by 40-60%. Start at onset of menses.

medications.name: Tranexamic Acid 500mg
medications.sig: 1-2 tablets (500-1000mg) three times daily for 3-5 days during menses (reduces blood loss by 40-60%)

medications.name: Ferrous Sulfate 200mg
medications.sig: 1 tablet twice daily for 3 months (treats iron deficiency anemia)

medications.name: Folic Acid 5mg
medications.sig: 1 tablet once daily for 3 months

highlights.label: Rule Out Pregnancy
highlights.text: Rule out pregnancy with serum/urine hCG before treatment. Pregnancy complications can cause bleeding.

highlights.label: Endometrial Biopsy Criteria
highlights.text: Endometrial biopsy indicated in women >45 years or with risk factors for endometrial cancer (obesity, PCOS, chronic anovulation, tamoxifen use).

highlights.label: Thrombosis Risk
highlights.text: Tranexamic acid increases thrombotic risk. Contraindicated in patients with history of DVT, PE, or hypercoagulable states.

highlights.label: Anemia Assessment
highlights.text: Evaluate for iron deficiency anemia with complete blood count and ferritin. Ferrous sulfate may cause GI upset – take with food.

highlights.label: Response
highlights.text: Expected reduction in bleeding within 24-48 hours. If no response, consider alternative diagnosis or structural cause.

regimens.name: Cycle Regulation (COCP)
regimens.description: Combined Oral Contraceptive Pill regulates menstrual cycles and prevents recurrence of AUB. Effective for long-term management.

medications.name: Combined Oral Contraceptive Pill (ethinyl estradiol 30-35mcg + progestin)
medications.sig: 1 tablet daily for 3-6 months (regulates cycle, prevents recurrence)

medications.name: Paracetamol 500mg
medications.sig: As needed for dysmenorrhea (painful periods)

highlights.label: COCP Contraindications
highlights.text: Avoid COCP if: >35 years + smoking, migraine with aura, thromboembolic risk, uncontrolled hypertension, breast cancer.

highlights.label: NSAID Option
highlights.text: NSAIDs (mefenamic acid, ibuprofen) can reduce menstrual blood loss by 20-30%. Consider if COCP contraindicated.

highlights.label: Lifestyle
highlights.text: Lifestyle modifications: weight management if obese, regular exercise. Levonorgestrel-releasing IUD (Mirena) is excellent long-term option.

regimens.name: Refractory Bleeding
regimens.description: If bleeding persists despite medical therapy, consider endometrial ablation or hysterectomy. Refer to gynecology for further evaluation.

highlights.label: Structural Causes
highlights.text: Consider pelvic ultrasound to exclude structural pathology (fibroids, polyps, adenomyosis). Evaluate for coagulopathies (von Willebrand disease) and thyroid dysfunction.

highlights.label: Referral Criteria
highlights.text: REFER IF: No response to medical therapy, persistent heavy bleeding, endometrial hyperplasia, or abnormal imaging findings.

prescriptions.name: H. pylori Infection in Pregnancy
prescriptions.summary: Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) infection in pregnancy requires careful management when treatment is indicated, such as in cases of severe hyperemesis gravidarum, active peptic ulcer disease, or documented infection with significant symptoms. Treatment decisions must balance maternal benefits against potential fetal risks, with antibiotic selection guided by trimester. Dual therapy with amoxicillin and a proton pump inhibitor (PPI) is the preferred first-line regimen across all trimesters due to its safety profile. Triple therapy with metronidazole is reserved for second/third trimester if dual therapy fails.

regimens.name: Dual Therapy (Amoxicillin + PPI) - All Trimesters
regimens.description: Preferred first-line regimen across all trimesters. Amoxicillin is safe (Category B) and PPI provides acid suppression. Dual therapy has good efficacy with minimal fetal risk.

medications.name: Amoxicillin 1000mg
medications.sig: 1 tablet three times daily for 14 days

medications.name: Omeprazole 40mg
medications.sig: 1 capsule twice daily for 14 days

highlights.label: Indications
highlights.text: Treat ONLY if: confirmed H. pylori + severe hyperemesis OR active peptic ulcer bleeding where benefit of treatment outweighs risk.

highlights.label: First Trimester Safety
highlights.text: Amoxicillin: Pregnancy Category B - safe and preferred. Omeprazole: Category C - use when benefits outweigh risks; limited data but generally safe.

highlights.label: Avoid Clarithromycin
highlights.text: Clarithromycin: Avoid in pregnancy (Category C, associated with miscarriage risk).

highlights.label: Avoid Tetracycline
highlights.text: Tetracycline: Contraindicated in pregnancy (Category D).

highlights.label: Test of Cure
highlights.text: Test of cure 4-6 weeks post-treatment with stool antigen or urea breath test.

highlights.label: Expected Outcome
highlights.text: Symptom improvement expected within 1-2 weeks. Complete resolution after 14-day course. If no improvement after 72 hours, reassess.

regimens.name: Triple Therapy (Amoxicillin + Metronidazole + PPI)
regimens.description: Use ONLY if Amoxicillin + PPI dual therapy has failed, and confirm patient is past the first trimester. Metronidazole is safe after first trimester.

medications.name: Amoxicillin 1000mg
medications.sig: 1 tablet three times daily for 14 days

medications.name: Metronidazole 500mg
medications.sig: 1 tablet twice daily for 14 days (use ONLY if Amoxicillin + PPI dual therapy has failed, and confirm patient is past first trimester)

medications.name: Omeprazole 40mg
medications.sig: Continue PPI twice daily

highlights.label: Trimester Check
highlights.text: Metronidazole is Category B - safe after first trimester. CONFIRM patient is past first trimester before prescribing.

highlights.label: Resistance
highlights.text: Metronidazole resistance is common. Consider culture and sensitivity if available.

highlights.label: Alternative Options
highlights.text: Retreatment options if eradication fails: consider clarithromycin-based triple therapy (postpartum) or bismuth-based quadruple therapy.

prescriptions.name: Acute Diarrhea in Children (<5 years)
prescriptions.summary: Acute diarrhea in children under 5 years is defined as ≥3 loose or watery stools in 24 hours, lasting <14 days. The leading cause is viral (rotavirus, norovirus, adenovirus), though bacterial (Shigella, Salmonella, Campylobacter) and parasitic (Giardia) causes should be considered in severe cases or those with dysentery. Management is stepwise based on dehydration severity: Plan A (no dehydration - home care with ORS, zinc, and continued feeding), Plan B (some dehydration - 75 ml/kg ORS over 4 hours in OPD), and Plan C (severe dehydration - IV Ringer's Lactate with hospital referral). Zinc supplementation for 14 days reduces duration and recurrence.

regimens.name: Plan A - No Dehydration (Home Care)
regimens.description: For children with no signs of dehydration. Home management with ORS, zinc, continued feeding, and close monitoring.

medications.name: ORS (Low-osmolarity) sachets
medications.sig: 1 sachet in 1 liter boiled cooled water. Give 50-100 ml after each loose stool (Plan A - No Dehydration)

medications.name: Zinc sulfate 20mg/5ml syrup
medications.sig: 2.5 ml (10mg) once daily for 14 days (for 1 year old; 20mg daily for children >6 months)

medications.name: Racecadotril 10mg sachet
medications.sig: 1 sachet three times daily for 3 days (if available - reduces stool output)

highlights.label: DO NOT GIVE
highlights.text: Loperamide (Imodium) - contraindicated in children (dangerous). Ibuprofen - risk of kidney injury with dehydration. Aspirin - Reye's syndrome.

highlights.label: Continue Feeding
highlights.text: Continue breastfeeding or formula. Rice porridge (kanji), mashed banana, khichdi, toast, yogurt (if >6 months). Small frequent meals.

highlights.label: Red Flags
highlights.text: Blood in stool, severe dehydration (sunken eyes, no urine >6 hours), unable to drink, fever >39°C for >48 hours, lethargy, abdominal distension. REFER URGENTLY.

highlights.label: Expected Outcome
highlights.text: ORS + Zinc: 3-5 days recovery. Add Racecadotril: 24-48 hours faster.

regimens.name: Plan B - Some Dehydration
regimens.description: For children with some dehydration (sunken eyes, reduced skin turgor, thirst, decreased urine output). Requires ORS rehydration over 4 hours.

medications.name: ORS - Plan B (Some Dehydration)
medications.sig: 75 ml/kg over 4 hours (e.g., 750 ml for 10 kg child) - sips every 5-10 minutes

medications.name: Zinc sulfate 20mg/5ml syrup
medications.sig: Continue zinc for 14 days

highlights.label: Monitor Response
highlights.text: Reassess after 4 hours. If still dehydrated, repeat ORS or escalate to Plan C. If improved, transition to Plan A.

highlights.label: Vomiting
highlights.text: If vomiting, give small sips every 5-10 minutes. If unable to drink, consider IV fluids.

regimens.name: Plan C - Severe Dehydration
regimens.description: For children with severe dehydration (sunken eyes, no urine >6 hours, lethargy, sunken fontanelle). Requires immediate IV fluids and hospitalization.

medications.name: IV Ringer's Lactate
medications.sig: 100 ml/kg total: <12 months: 30 ml/kg over 1 hr, then 70 ml/kg over 5 hrs; >12 months: 30 ml/kg over 30 min, then 70 ml/kg over 2.5 hrs

highlights.label: HOSPITAL REFERRAL
highlights.text: Immediate hospitalization required. Monitor urine output, vital signs, and hydration status closely.

highlights.label: IV Access
highlights.text: If unable to get IV access, consider intraosseous (IO) line. Monitor for signs of fluid overload.

regimens.name: Dysentery Protocol
regimens.description: For children with blood in stool (dysentery). Requires antibiotics directed at Shigella, Salmonella, or Campylobacter.

medications.name: Azithromycin 200mg/5ml suspension
medications.sig: 10-20 mg/kg once daily for 3-5 days (for dysentery or bacterial infection)

highlights.label: Stool Culture
highlights.text: Send stool culture and sensitivity before starting antibiotics. Monitor for worsening symptoms.

highlights.label: Alternative Antibiotics
highlights.text: Ciprofloxacin 15 mg/kg/dose BID × 3 days is alternative. Ceftriaxone IV 50-80 mg/kg IV once daily for severe bacterial suspected.

highlights.label: Differential
highlights.text: Amebiasis: Bloody diarrhea with mucus ('currant jelly'), no fever. Treat with Metronidazole 35-50 mg/kg/day divided TID × 7-10 days.

prescriptions.name: Dysmenorrhea
prescriptions.summary: Dysmenorrhea is defined as painful menstrual cramps of uterine origin, typically beginning 1-2 days before or at the onset of menses, and lasting 1-3 days. It is classified as primary (no underlying pelvic pathology, common in adolescents 6-12 months after menarche) or secondary (associated with pelvic pathology such as endometriosis, adenomyosis, fibroids, PID, or IUD). First-line treatment involves NSAIDs started 1-2 days before menses, combined with heat therapy. Combined Oral Contraceptive Pills (COCP) are second-line for moderate-severe cases or when NSAIDs are insufficient.

regimens.name: NSAID Therapy
regimens.description: First-line treatment for dysmenorrhea. NSAIDs inhibit prostaglandin synthesis, reducing uterine contractions and pain. Start 1-2 days before menses.

medications.name: Mefenamic Acid 500mg
medications.sig: 1 tablet three times daily with food. Start 1-2 days before menses, continue for 3-5 days.

medications.name: Heat therapy (hot water bottle)
medications.sig: Apply to lower abdomen during menses

highlights.label: Start BEFORE Menses
highlights.text: Start NSAID 1-2 days BEFORE period expected - more effective than waiting for pain to start. Take with food to prevent GI upset.

highlights.label: Contraindications
highlights.text: Avoid NSAIDs in patients with peptic ulcer or renal disease. Use with caution in patients on anticoagulants.

highlights.label: Primary vs Secondary
highlights.text: Secondary causes (endometriosis, adenomyosis, PID) present with: pain >25 years, pain >3 days, dyspareunia, irregular bleeding, infertility, abnormal pelvic exam.

highlights.label: Expected Outcome
highlights.text: Pain relief within 30-60 minutes. If no relief after 3 cycles, consider COCP or evaluate for secondary causes.

regimens.name: Combined Oral Contraceptive Pill
regimens.description: Second-line for moderate-severe dysmenorrhea or when NSAIDs insufficient. COCP suppresses ovulation and reduces prostaglandin production.

medications.name: Combined Oral Contraceptive Pill (COCP)
medications.sig: 1 tablet daily for 21-28 days. Duration: 3-6 cycles (then reassess). Indicated if NSAIDs insufficient.

medications.name: Vitamin E 400 IU
medications.sig: 1 capsule daily during menses for 3-5 days (supportive therapy)

highlights.label: COCP Contraindications
highlights.text: Avoid COCP if: >35 years + smoking, migraine with aura, thromboembolic risk, uncontrolled hypertension, breast cancer.

highlights.label: Side Effects
highlights.text: COCP may cause nausea, breast tenderness, mood changes, breakthrough bleeding. Usually resolve within 1-3 cycles.

highlights.label: Expected Outcome
highlights.text: 60-90% reduction in pain after 3-6 cycles. Reassess need for continued use.

regimens.name: Supportive & Lifestyle
regimens.description: Lifestyle modifications and supportive therapies that reduce menstrual pain. Regular exercise, dietary changes, and stress reduction improve symptoms.

medications.name: Magnesium 200mg
medications.sig: 1 tablet daily for 3 months (supportive therapy)

highlights.label: Lifestyle
highlights.text: Regular aerobic exercise (20-30 min, 3-4 times/week). Dietary modifications: reduce salt, caffeine, alcohol; increase fruits, vegetables.

highlights.label: Non-pharmacological
highlights.text: TENS, acupuncture, cognitive behavioral therapy, relaxation techniques. Vitamin D supplementation if deficiency present.

prescriptions.name: Pregnancy Constipation
prescriptions.summary: Constipation in pregnancy is a common condition defined as infrequent bowel movements (<3 per week), hard stools, and straining, affecting up to 40% of pregnant women. It is caused by hormonal changes (increased progesterone), mechanical compression by the growing uterus, and iron supplementation. First-line treatment involves lifestyle modifications (increased fiber, hydration, exercise) and fiber supplements. Polyethylene Glycol 3350 (PEG) is the preferred osmotic laxative as it is minimally absorbed and safe in pregnancy. Lactulose is a safe alternative.

regimens.name: Lifestyle + Fiber
regimens.description: First-line treatment for pregnancy constipation. Lifestyle modifications are safe and effective. Fiber supplements if dietary fiber insufficient.

medications.name: Psyllium husk (Ispaghol) 6g
medications.sig: 1 tablespoon in 1 glass of water ONCE daily. Must be taken with adequate water to avoid obstruction.

highlights.label: STRICTLY AVOID
highlights.text: Castor oil (uterine stimulation risk). Mineral oil (reduced vitamin absorption, risk of neonatal bleeding). Senna (genotoxicity concerns). Magnesium citrate/sodium phosphate (electrolyte imbalance).

highlights.label: Adequate Water
highlights.text: Fiber supplements MUST be taken with adequate water (1 glass minimum) to avoid obstruction. Increase to 8-12 cups (2-3 liters) water daily.

highlights.label: Lifestyle
highlights.text: Increase fiber intake to 25-30g daily (fruits, vegetables, whole grains, legumes). Drink 8-12 cups water daily. Daily walking or exercise (20-30 minutes). Regular toileting routine (especially after meals).

highlights.label: Expected Outcome
highlights.text: Lifestyle changes + fiber: Improvement in 2-7 days.

regimens.name: Osmotic Laxative (PEG or Lactulose)
regimens.description: Second-line if lifestyle + fiber fails. Polyethylene Glycol 3350 is preferred by ACOG and AGA. Minimally absorbed and safe in pregnancy.

medications.name: Polyethylene Glycol 3350 (PEG) 17g powder
medications.sig: 1 sachet (17g) dissolved in 250-500ml water ONCE daily. Duration: 2-4 weeks, then reassess. Preferred by ACOG and AGA. Onset: 24-72 hours.

highlights.label: Safety
highlights.text: PEG is NOT absorbed systemically. Preferred by ACOG and AGA for pregnancy constipation. Safe for long-term use.

highlights.label: Alternative
highlights.text: Lactulose 15-30ml (10-20g) ONCE daily is alternative if PEG unavailable. Onset: 24-48 hours.

highlights.label: Expected Outcome
highlights.text: PEG or Lactulose: Bowel movement in 24-72 hours. Full response: 1-2 weeks with consistent treatment.

regimens.name: Stool Softener (Docusate)
regimens.description: Third-line if second-line fails after 1-2 weeks. Docusate sodium is a stool softener. Considered safe in pregnancy but less effective than osmotic laxatives.

medications.name: Docusate Sodium 100mg
medications.sig: 1 tablet twice daily (stool softener – considered safe if second-line fails after 1-2 weeks)

highlights.label: Red Flags
highlights.text: REFER URGENTLY: No bowel movement for 1 week despite treatment, severe abdominal pain, rectal bleeding, fever, signs of obstruction (vomiting, distension, no flatus).

highlights.label: Iron Supplements
highlights.text: Iron supplements can worsen constipation – consider switching to a different formulation or reducing dose.

highlights.label: Risk Factors
highlights.text: Constipation is most common in first and third trimesters. Women with history of constipation or pelvic floor dysfunction are at higher risk.

prescriptions.name: Neuropathic Pain (Peripheral Neuropathy)
prescriptions.summary: Peripheral neuropathy is a length-dependent, stocking-glove distribution of nerve damage characterized by burning pain, tingling, numbness, and night worsening. Common causes include diabetes mellitus, vitamin B12 deficiency, alcohol, hypothyroidism, uremia, and drug toxicity. First-line treatment according to NICE guidelines includes pregabalin, gabapentin, or duloxetine, chosen based on patient profile and comorbidities. Treatment requires gradual titration and 4-6 weeks to assess response. Secondary causes must be investigated and treated simultaneously.

regimens.name: Pregabalin (First-Line Option A)
regimens.description: First-line treatment for neuropathic pain. Pregabalin binds to alpha-2-delta subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels, reducing neurotransmitter release. Start low and titrate slowly.

medications.name: Pregabalin 75mg
medications.sig: Start 75mg at bedtime for 7 days, then 75mg twice daily for 7 days, then 150mg twice daily. Max 600mg/day. Duration: 4-6 weeks, then reassess.

highlights.label: Diagnostic Workup
highlights.text: Must rule out causes: Diabetes (HbA1c), Vitamin B12 deficiency (B12 level), Alcohol (LFTs), Hypothyroidism (TSH, T4), Uremia (Creatinine, BUN), Drugs (isoniazid, metronidazole, vincristine).

highlights.label: Red Flags
highlights.text: REFER URGENTLY: Rapidly progressive weakness, asymmetric neuropathy, autonomic symptoms, unexplained weight loss/fever, history of cancer, bowel/bladder dysfunction, no improvement after 6 weeks.

highlights.label: Side Effects
highlights.text: Common: dizziness, somnolence, peripheral edema, weight gain. Start low and titrate slowly. Take bedtime dose first to minimize daytime drowsiness.

highlights.label: Withdrawal
highlights.text: Do NOT stop abruptly. Taper gradually over 1-2 weeks to prevent withdrawal symptoms (insomnia, headache, nausea).

highlights.label: Expected Outcome
highlights.text: 2 weeks: Initial response. 4-6 weeks: Full effect. 3 months: Reassess and adjust.

regimens.name: Gabapentin (First-Line Option B)
regimens.description: First-line alternative to pregabalin. Gabapentin has similar mechanism and efficacy. May be preferred in patients with renal impairment or for cost reasons.

medications.name: Gabapentin 100mg
medications.sig: Start 100mg three times daily. Increase weekly: 300mg TID, 600mg TID, 900mg TID. Max 3600mg/day. Duration: 4-6 weeks, then reassess.

highlights.label: Renal Dosing
highlights.text: Gabapentin is renally excreted. Dose adjustment needed in renal impairment (eGFR <60). Start with lower doses and titrate slowly.

highlights.label: Alternative
highlights.text: May have fewer drug interactions than pregabalin. Consider in patients on multiple medications.

regimens.name: Duloxetine (First-Line Option C)
regimens.description: SNRI antidepressant with proven efficacy in neuropathic pain. Preferred in patients with comorbid depression or diabetic neuropathy.

medications.name: Duloxetine 30mg
medications.sig: 30mg once daily for 7 days, then increase to 60mg once daily. Max 120mg/day. Duration: 4-6 weeks, then reassess. Indicated for neuropathic pain with depression, diabetic neuropathy.

highlights.label: Side Effects
highlights.text: Common: nausea, dry mouth, somnolence, dizziness, insomnia. Take with food to reduce nausea. Start with 30mg for 1 week to improve tolerability.

highlights.label: Suicide Risk
highlights.text: Monitor for worsening depression, suicidal thoughts, especially in young adults (18-24 years).

highlights.label: Diabetic Neuropathy
highlights.text: Duloxetine is specifically indicated for diabetic neuropathy. Tight glycemic control (HbA1c <7%) is essential.

regimens.name: Cause-Specific Therapy
regimens.description: Treat underlying cause of neuropathy. Essential for long-term management. Vitamin B12 deficiency, diabetic neuropathy, and alcohol-related neuropathy have specific treatments.

medications.name: Methylcobalamin 1500mcg
medications.sig: 1 tablet once daily for 1 month, then 1500mcg once weekly for 2 months (for Vitamin B12 deficiency)

medications.name: Vitamin B Complex
medications.sig: 1 tablet once daily for 3 months

highlights.label: B12 Deficiency
highlights.text: Vitamin B12 deficiency: Methylcobalamin 1500mcg daily for 1 month, then weekly for 2 months. Check B12 levels and treat aggressively.

highlights.label: Diabetic Neuropathy
highlights.text: Tight glycemic control (HbA1c <7%) + Gabapentin or Duloxetine. Alpha-lipoic acid 600mg daily has modest benefit.

highlights.label: Alcohol-Related
highlights.text: Stop alcohol + Thiamine 100mg daily + Folic acid 5mg daily for 1 month.

highlights.label: NSAIDs
highlights.text: DO NOT GIVE: NSAIDs (ineffective for neuropathic pain). Opioids as first-line (limited efficacy, risk of dependence). Corticosteroids (unless inflammatory cause confirmed).

prescriptions.name: Female Infertility (Anovulatory/PCOS)

patient.notes: BMI 28, PCOS, anovulatory cycles, no tubal/male factor, trying >6 months

prescriptions.summary: Primary infertility due to anovulatory PCOS. Regular cycles >6 months, BMI <30. No evidence of tubal blockage or male factor infertility. Patient is 28 years old with confirmed PCOS by Rotterdam criteria. Normal AMH, TSH, and prolactin levels. Partner semen analysis normal.

regimens.name: Letrozole First-Line Therapy
regimens.description: Evidence-based first-line ovulation induction for PCOS-related infertility. Superior to clomiphene with higher pregnancy rates, better endometrial thickness, and lower multiple pregnancy risk.

medications.name: Letrozole
medications.sig: Take 1 tablet (2.5 mg) by mouth once daily on cycle days 3 through 7. Track menstrual cycles and use LH ovulation predictor kits starting day 10. Timed intercourse every 2 days between days 12-16 or as directed by LH surge.

medications.name: Folic Acid
medications.sig: Take 1 tablet (5 mg) by mouth once daily with food. Essential for neural tube defect prevention in early pregnancy.

medications.name: Vitamin D3
medications.sig: Take 1 capsule (2000 IU) by mouth once daily with meals. Supports overall reproductive health and ovarian function.

highlights.label: Pregnancy Test Required
highlights.text: Confirm negative pregnancy test before each cycle. Letrozole is category X in pregnancy. Perform serum β-hCG or urine pregnancy test at cycle start.

highlights.label: Multiple Pregnancy Risk
highlights.text: Multiple pregnancy rate: 5-8% with letrozole (lower than clomiphene 10-15%). Still, counsel patient on risks of twins. Ultrasound monitoring recommended if possible.

highlights.label: Ovarian Hyperstimulation
highlights.text: OHSS risk is low with letrozole (<2%) but still possible. Monitor for symptoms: severe pelvic pain, nausea, vomiting, weight gain. Report immediately.

highlights.label: Timing
highlights.text: Most fertile window: 12-16 days after period starts. Use LH predictor kits. Ovulation usually occurs 5-10 days after last dose (cycle days 9-14). Timing intercourse every 2-3 days maximizes chances.

highlights.label: Side Effects
highlights.text: Common: hot flashes (up to 30%), headache (20%), mood changes, dizziness, fatigue. Usually mild and transient. Counsel that these are temporary. Severe side effects are rare.

highlights.label: Ovulation Rate
highlights.text: Ovulation rate: 31.3-41.3% per cycle. Pregnancy rate: up to 33.8% per cycle if ovulation occurs. Cumulative pregnancy rate: 60-70% over 6 cycles.

highlights.label: Evidence
highlights.text: Meta-analysis of 7 studies (n=1,200+) confirmed letrozole significantly improves pregnancy rates (RR 1.50, 95% CI: 1.28-1.77) and ovulation rates (RR 1.29, 95% CI: 1.15-1.44) vs clomiphene in PCOS patients. Combination regimen shows highest ovulation rate of 41.3%.

highlights.label: Expected Outcome
highlights.text: Cycles 1-3: 40-50% ovulation rate. Cycles 4-6: cumulative pregnancy rate 60-70%. If no pregnancy after 6 cycles, refer for IVF evaluation.

highlights.label: BMI Target
highlights.text: Target BMI: 18.5-24.9. Weight loss of 5-10% if overweight significantly improves ovulation rates. Even 5% weight loss can restore ovulation in 60% of overweight women with PCOS.

highlights.label: Lifestyle
highlights.text: Recommend 30 minutes of walking daily. Stop smoking, limit alcohol. Track menstrual cycles meticulously. Use LH ovulation predictor kits from day 10. Consider basal body temperature charting.

regimens.followUp: Monitor with mid-luteal progesterone (day 21) to confirm ovulation. If no ovulation after 3 cycles, consider dose increase to 5 mg or combination therapy. Perform pelvic ultrasound before each cycle if available. Reassess every 2-3 cycles.

regimens.name: Combination Therapy (Letrozole + Clomiphene)
regimens.description: For patients who fail letrozole alone after 3-6 cycles. Highest ovulation rate (41.3%) and pregnancy rate (33.8%) reported with this combination.

medications.name: Letrozole
medications.sig: Take 1 tablet (2.5 mg) by mouth once daily on cycle days 3 through 7.

medications.name: Clomiphene Citrate
medications.sig: Take 1 tablet (50 mg) by mouth once daily on cycle days 5 through 9. Start monitoring with ovulation predictor kits from day 10.

medications.name: Folic Acid
medications.sig: Continue folic acid 5 mg daily.

highlights.label: Higher Multiple Risk
highlights.text: Combination therapy increases multiple pregnancy risk to 10-15%. Close monitoring with ultrasound is strongly recommended. Consider canceling cycle if >3 mature follicles develop.

highlights.label: OHSS Risk
highlights.text: OHSS risk increases with combination therapy. Monitor closely for symptoms: severe pelvic pain, nausea, vomiting, rapid weight gain (>2 lbs/day), shortness of breath.

highlights.label: Anti-estrogenic Effects
highlights.text: Clomiphene may reduce endometrial thickness and cervical mucus quality. Consider estrogen supplementation if endometrial thickness <. Counsel on these effects.

highlights.label: Visual Disturbances
highlights.text: Clomiphene can cause visual symptoms (blurred vision, scotomas) in 1.5% of patients. Discontinue immediately if visual changes occur. Notify physician.

highlights.label: Evidence
highlights.text: Combination therapy showed the highest ovulation rate (41.3%) and pregnancy rate (33.8%) among all regimens in a 2025 meta-analysis. Consider if letrozole alone is insufficient.

highlights.label: Alternative
highlights.text: If combination therapy fails after 6 cycles, refer to fertility specialist for gonadotropin therapy or IVF. Success rates with IVF in PCOS patients exceed 60% in this age group.

regimens.followUp: Ultrasound monitoring for follicle tracking and endometrial thickness. Mid-luteal progesterone for ovulation confirmation. Monthly review. Reassess after 3 cycles. If no success, refer to reproductive specialist.

regimens.name: Metformin Addition (For Obese PCOS)
regimens.description: For PCOS patients with BMI >27 or insulin resistance. Metformin improves ovulation and pregnancy rates when added to letrozole, particularly in obese patients.

medications.name: Letrozole
medications.sig: Take 1 tablet (2.5 mg) by mouth once daily on cycle days 3 through 7.

medications.name: Metformin HCl
medications.sig: Take 1 tablet (500 mg) by mouth twice daily with meals. Start at 500 mg once daily for 1 week, then increase to 500 mg twice daily. Titrate up to 1000 mg twice daily as tolerated.

medications.name: Folic Acid
medications.sig: Continue folic acid 5 mg daily.

highlights.label: GI Side Effects
highlights.text: Metformin commonly causes GI distress (nausea, diarrhea, metallic taste). Start with low dose (500 mg once daily) and titrate slowly over 4-6 weeks. Extended-release formulation may be better tolerated.

highlights.label: Vitamin B12 Deficiency
highlights.text: Long-term metformin use causes B12 deficiency. Monitor B12 annually. Consider supplementation if deficient. Counsel on long-term monitoring.

highlights.label: Renal Function
highlights.text: Check baseline renal function. Contraindicated if eGFR . Use with caution if eGFR 30-45. Monitor creatinine periodically.

highlights.label: Weight Loss Benefit
highlights.text: Metformin promotes modest weight loss (2-3 kg). Combine with lifestyle changes for best results. Weight loss improves ovulation rates independently.

highlights.label: Evidence
highlights.text: Metformin plus letrozole improves ovulation rates in obese PCOS patients compared to letrozole alone. Particularly beneficial in women with insulin resistance (HOMA-IR >2.5).

highlights.label: Clinical Trial Data
highlights.text: Studies show 60-70% ovulation rate and 40-50% pregnancy rate over 6 cycles with metformin plus letrozole in obese PCOS. Especially effective when combined with lifestyle modification.

regimens.followUp: Monitor HbA1c and fasting glucose at 3 months. Check B12 annually. Renal function at baseline and yearly. Review weight and ovulation response at each visit.
